_presentation_note:
REVISED 2026-08-16 on Daniel's call, and this is the important axis. A first pass listed every act by name with a face attached, which meant inventing a flavour difference between Dan Steele and DF Funk that rested on a face chair the workbook itself marks 'assumed'. Daniel's correction: some of these are genuinely fronted and some are interchangeable, so do not name the interchangeable ones. Name them and you have promised a personality the booking cannot guarantee. Spec them and you have promised a sound, a size and a price, which is what you can actually deliver.

Two values:
  presentation: "face"  the person IS the product. Publishes name and face.
  presentation: "spec"  the format IS the product. Publishes instrumentation, never a name.

This is ORTHOGONAL to status (flagship/listing). Jazz Duo is a spec'd format with a full flagship page.

_facets_note: ADDED 2026-09-16 with the new-act skill. Every filterable fact about an act is a tag against a vocabulary declared here, the same contract buckets[] and rateCard[] already had: bucket_tags = the kind of night, config_tags = the size, genre_tags = the genre, vocals = whether a singer fronts it, area_tags = where it plays. A select renders on the roster page only for a facet the roster actually varies on, and only with the options some act carries, so an unused tag is never a dead filter. vocals is one of: sung (a singer fronts it), instrumental (no singer), optional (a voice can be added; matches both filters). area_tags omitted means every area in areas[], which is the roster-wide default; set it only on an act that does not travel the whole list, and the Where filter appears the moment one does. The vocabularies grow with the roster; never publish a count of them either. UPDATED 2026-09-23: occasion_tags (against occasions[]) joined the facets; the Occasion select renders on the roster the same way the others do. The 'dj' bucket was retired the same day.

identity: One act, three sizes. This is the only booking on the roster that changes shape during the night instead of being replaced.

The reason to care is the contract. Most events buy the front of the night and the back of the night from two different acts, which means two load-ins, two sound checks, two sets of names to keep straight and a seam in the middle that guests can hear. This ladders instead: a duo through arrival and dinner, then the rhythm section arrives and the same voice fronts the dance floor. The party sees one band getting bigger.
At quartet it stops being a cocktail act. The full rhythm section behind one voice, keys or a second guitar on top, playing a covers set built for a floor.
It is a premium cover band. It is not a show band. Nobody changes costume, there is no choreography and there is no host segment. The band plays, reads the floor, and plays the next thing.
This is a named act, published under the name of the person who fronts it, and any substitution in the lineup is named to you in advance.

identity: This is the cocktail hour booking. Upright bass and guitar, playing the standards book, at a volume you can talk across.

It is sold as a format rather than under a name, and that is a deliberate promise. What you are buying for this hour is an instrumentation, a repertoire and a volume. Which two musicians deliver it does not change any of the three, and pretending otherwise would mean naming a pair we cannot guarantee for your date. You get the spec, on every date it is available.

Most of what goes wrong in the first two hours of an event is a volume decision, not a repertoire decision. A band that plays this hour at the level it plays the dance floor makes guests shout at each other while they are still deciding what kind of night it is. A duo is the honest instrument for it: two musicians cannot get loud by accident, and the arrangement stays open enough that conversation sits on top of it.
Standards are the repertoire because they are the one set of songs nobody has to be told about. Guests do not identify the tunes and do not need to. The night reads as expensive and unhurried.
The duo covers arrival, cocktails and dinner on one line of the contract. If the night also needs a dance floor, that is a second booking.

identity: Flamenco is the booking on this roster that almost nobody else in Colorado sells as a private event product. It exists here as a concert act, or as a guitarist playing Spanish-flavored background. Dirty Flamenco is neither. It is a working group with a standing repertoire, sold at private event scale.

Most live music at a private event is designed to be felt and not watched. This is the opposite booking, and its work is the set moment: a cultural centerpiece, a corporate dinner that has to be memorable, a reception that wants something guests will describe to people who were not there.

The repertoire is palos, the traditional forms, not a set of pop songs with nylon strings on them. That is the difference between a flamenco booking and a Spanish guitar booking, and it is audible inside eight bars.
This is a named act rather than a format, an existing group booked under its own name. Any change to the lineup is named to you in advance.

acts.meta_description: Blues and rock for private events in Denver and the Colorado mountains. Solo through four piece, fronted by Tony Medina. Send a date and we price the night.
identity: Some nights want a voice that sounds like it has been somewhere. Tony Medina sings with grit and gravel in it and plays guitar with a funk guitarist's right hand, which is why a set of blues and classic rock in his hands tends to catch a crowd that thought it had turned up for background music.

The book is the blues and most of what the blues turned into. Freddie King and B.B. King at one end, The Cars, Prince and the rock records of the seventies and nineties at the other, and his own songs threaded through. Guests recognise nearly all of it without being told what it is, which is the whole trick of a covers set at a private event.

It scales from one musician to four. Solo it is a voice and an acoustic guitar, warm enough to sit under conversation through welcome drinks and dinner. Add percussion, then bass and drums, and at the four piece it is a band with a floor in front of it.

He is a working Denver musician with his own catalogue, his own site and his own channel, so none of this has to be taken on trust. The footage on this page is his, and there is a great deal more of it where that came from.
This is a named act, published under the name of the person who fronts it, and any substitution in the lineup is named to you in advance.

identity: Last Consulate is the solo project of one multi-instrumentalist, built on upright bass, electric bass, guitar and downtempo electronics.

The improvising is jazz. The production is early-2000s downtempo electronica, the slow and hazy end of it, instrumental and warm, and mixed so that what was played and what was sampled are hard to tell apart.
Upright bass is the lead instrument. Under it sit slow hip-hop drums, extended jazz harmony, tape-worn keys and delayed guitars, and the improvised bass line is usually the melody.
It is built for arrival, cocktails and dinner, played at a volume guests can talk across, with the feel of a late jazz set or a hotel lobby.

identity: Changes is a guitar trio with a modern edge. Doug Emery on guitar, Sri Viswanath on fretless bass and Brian Jaffe on drums, playing the standards the way a working trio plays them, with the arrangements left open and a little risk in the solos. It holds a dinner at conversation volume, and it holds a listening crowd when the night wants that instead.

The three musicians are the reason it books under a name. Doug studied guitar performance at Berklee, played more than three thousand dates across New England, from jazz duos to wedding bands, and now teaches music full time in Denver. Sri spent decades as a working bassist in New York, on stages from Smalls to the Plaza Hotel, and played on Radha Thomas's 2019 tribute to Chet Baker. Brian came through the Lamont School of Music at the University of Denver and has played more than a hundred theater productions in the Denver pit orchestras since 2011.

It books as a trio, or as a quartet with a saxophone out front when the night wants a horn on the melody. The trio is the cocktail hour and dinner size. The quartet is the one for a featured set at a gala, or a client dinner where the music is part of the program.
Their own site carries the three bios and two studio recordings, and the recordings are the quickest way to hear what the trio sounds like before you write to us.
This is a named act, booked under the names of the three musicians in it, and if anyone in the lineup changes, we tell you in advance.

acts.blurb: A sound bath for your team, offsite or retreat. Your people lie down in low light for seventy-five minutes with nothing to do and nothing to say, with live instruments played over composed music and bass deep enough to feel in your chest, and Firstwater opens and closes the session with ceremony. Firstwater brings it to your venue or holds it in a partner space in Denver, and it books for wellness weeks, team building days, retreats and transition days.
acts._identity_note: Written in the Signet voice from the act's own published lines and read aloud against AI-TELLS Layer 7 on 2026-09-19: no fragment closers, no trailing appositives, contractions throughout, and the trade words the act's site uses (a composed bed, sub-bass, the rig) expanded into words a planner owns (music composed for it, bass deep enough to feel in your chest, the sound system). Rewritten the same day on Daniel's rulings: no name anywhere, buyer search terms (sound bath, sound healing, corporate sound bath, team building) in place of 'sound sessions'. 'Sound healing' is a search keyword here under BASE-VOICE's term-of-art allowance, used where the page's job needs it and nowhere as a claim. The lines that are the act's own stay verbatim: 'strong enough to feel in your chest and soft enough to rest inside', 'nobody is asked to share, to speak, or to be anywhere but on the floor', 'the month a team earned something quiet', 'if you have a space, we can make it sound like a different one'.
identity: Firstwater is a sound bath led by one facilitator, and if you've been to one you already know how to arrive: lie down, get warm, and rest. The facilitator composes the music for each session, plays live instruments over it, and mixes the whole thing from the floor, lying where your people will lie. The facilitator treats the venue like a studio and tunes the sound system to it, so if you have a space, Firstwater can make it sound like a different one.

Your people come in to low light and lie down, and the mats and blankets are already there. The session opens with ceremony, then there are seventy-five minutes of sound strong enough to feel in your chest and soft enough to rest inside, with real silence partway through, and it closes the same way. Nobody is asked to share, to speak, or to be anywhere but on the floor. Some people follow the guidance closely, some drift, and some sleep, and each of those is a fine way to spend the hour. Afterward there's tea near the door, and people stay awhile or slip out as they please.

Companies book it as a corporate sound bath three ways: a team session at your office or in a partner space in Denver, one or more sessions built into an offsite or a retreat, and a transition day, with a session for the people leaving a company and for the team that stays. As a group sound healing session it suits a wellness week or a team building day, and it's for hospitals, hospices, libraries, schools and conference organizers as much as for companies and event planners. Couples book it too, as a private sound bath for a wedding weekend or a bachelorette, at the house they rented or a partner space in Denver. Firstwater brings the sound system, the mats, the blankets and the waivers, and what it needs from you is enough floor for your people to lie down, a standard outlet, and about ninety minutes ahead of doors.

Firstwater's own site is where to read about the public sound baths it holds around Denver and the Front Range, the plain answers to what happens at one, and a journal written in the facilitator's own words.
This is a named act. What you book is Firstwater, and the one facilitator behind the name is the one who arrives with the sound system and runs the session.

identity: René Moffatt writes the songs he sings. He's a folk and Americana songwriter based just outside Denver, with six records behind him, King of the Mountain and Here and Now Is Home among them, and an NPR Tiny Desk Contest entry every year since 2019. He calls it heady folk for the open-hearted, and the company he keeps on a playlist is Josh Ritter, Jeff Tweedy and The Avett Brothers.

Solo, it's a voice and an acoustic guitar. It plays under welcome drinks and on a patio at a volume people talk across, and it's the right size for a dinner party or a retreat evening where the songs are the point of the night. He's played the listening venues around Denver, Swallow Hill and the Black Rose Acoustic Society among them, and stages at the Denver Botanic Gardens and the Clyfford Still Museum.

With the band, René Moffatt & The Moonshadows, the same songs get lead guitar, bass and drums under them. The duo is his voice and guitar with a lead guitar beside it, the trio adds bass, and the four piece adds drums, which is the band you can watch on a Denver club stage and at the Underground Music Showcase in the footage below. They played the Boulder Roots Music Fest as well, and that size is the one for a park stage or a summer party.

His own songs lead a set. He plays covers beside them when a night wants them, and the ones on his channel run from Willie Nelson to The Beatles and The Cars, so tell us the balance you want and he builds the set to it.
This is a named act, booked under the name of the person who fronts it, and if anyone in the lineup changes, we tell you in advance.

_occasions_note: ADDED 2026-09-23. occasion_tags are the site's own four trees (weddings, corporate, private parties, daytime), tagged from what each act's page says it plays, so the Occasion filter on /music/ answers the question the rest of the site is organised by. An act with no page is tagged from its blurb. The occasion hubs can deep-link the roster pre-filtered with ?occasion=<id>.
_lanes_note: ADDED 2026-09-23. The roster page shows two lanes, and `lane` is which one an act sits in: 'format' (a configuration sold on instrumentation, the spec'd acts) or 'named' (an act booked by its name). It is NOT the same axis as `presentation`: Firstwater, Last Consulate and Your Bird Can Sing are spec'd (nobody is named) and still named acts, because what you book is that act. When `lane` is omitted it follows presentation: face = named, spec = format. The filter, the contact picker, the HTML sitemap and the sibling lists all read the lane.
_entity_note: ADDED 2026-09-23. `entity` on a named act emits a Person or MusicGroup node in the structured data, on the roster and on the act's page, with sameAs to the act's own site and channel where they are known. That is the named-act promise ('a name you can look up') stated in markup. Firstwater carries none on Daniel's ruling that nothing about the person crosses to Signet; Last Consulate and Your Bird Can Sing carry a MusicGroup node with no sameAs, since neither publishes a site.
_card_line_note: ADDED 2026-09-23. A format-lane card on /music/ is compact (no media) and prints `card_line` when present, else the first sentence of the blurb. The full blurb still renders on the act page, in llms.txt and in the Service description; nothing is shortened at source.
